More disturbing is the contention that a recent development negates the viability of the section 409 alternative. The forwarders state that long-haul carriers have been buying up local or short-haul carriers and then, assertedly, refusing to enter into contracts with freight forwarders at reasonable 51 The forwarders' evidentiary presentation on this rates. point consisted of a recitation of the numbers of contracts cancelled by motor carriers or discontinued due to the exorbitant rates of motor carriers. It is difficult to evaluate this evidence, however, since it may be normal for these contracts to be frequently cancelled and renegotiated, especially during times of rising costs and inflation. Nor is there any comparison offered indicating the proportion of cancelled contracts to those outstanding. Thus it is difficult to assess whether the forwarders have other motor carrier service options available. If this is a real problem, the substantial terminal area expansion contemplated by the rules adopted in this proceeding should greatly mitigate its seriousness. We also tend to discount the need to take special measures to solve this problem, since an examination of the list of participants in this proceeding indicates a plethora of independent short-haul carriers which should be available for assembly and distribution beyond terminal areas at compensatory rates.
As has been stated several times in this proceeding, we believe that the benefits of administrative simplicity and public comprehension gained through uniform treatment
It is argued that long-haul motor carriers are competitors of freight forwarders for less-than-truckload traffic, and, therefore, long-haul owners of short-haul carriers have a strong disincentive to offering reasonable section 409 contract rates to freight forwarders.
